Collinearity diagnostics table

Source: R/collinearity.R
apa_collinearity.Rd

Makes an APA-style table of the variance inflation factor (VIF) and tolerance of each predictor in a regression model, as computed by performance::check_collinearity().

Usage

apa_collinearity(
  x,
  columns = c("VIF", "VIF_CI", "Tolerance"),
  flag = NULL,
  ci = 0.95,
  format_variable_names = TRUE,
  digits = 2,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

a regression model with at least two predictors (any model that performance::check_collinearity() accepts, e.g., lm, glm, lme4, glmmTMB, or pscl models), or the output of performance::check_collinearity()

columns

columns to display, in order: any of "VIF", "VIF_CI" (confidence interval of VIF), "SE_factor" (\(\sqrt{VIF}\), the factor by which the standard error is inflated), "Tolerance", and "Tolerance_CI"

flag

NULL (default) or a number: VIFs at or above it are bolded (e.g., flag = 5 or flag = 10), and the note says so

ci

confidence level of the intervals

format_variable_names

if TRUE (default), term names are formatted as in apa_parameters() (e.g., "factor(cyl)" becomes "Cyl", and "wt:hp" becomes "Wt \(\times\) Hp"). Set to FALSE to keep the names exactly as performance::check_collinearity() gives them.

digits

number of decimal places (unaffected by apa7_defaults(accuracy = ))

...

arguments passed to performance::check_collinearity() (e.g., component)

Value

apa7_tbl (tibble)

Details

The VIF of a predictor is the factor by which the variance of its coefficient is inflated by its correlations with the other predictors. Tolerance is 1/VIF, the proportion of the predictor's variance that the other predictors do not explain. Common rules of thumb treat VIFs above 5 or 10 as signs of problematic collinearity; flag bolds them.

For terms with more than 1 degree of freedom (e.g., factors with more than two levels), VIF is the generalized VIF (Fox & Monette, 1992), and "SE_factor" is \(GVIF^{1/(2df)}\), which is comparable across terms with different degrees of freedom. The note names these terms.

In models with interactions, the VIFs of the interaction and its component terms are high in part because product terms are correlated with their components. This kind of collinearity does not affect the test of the interaction, and centering the predictors reduces it. When any of these VIFs is at or above flag (or 5, if flag is NULL), the note says so.

Models with several parts (e.g., the count and zero-inflation models of pscl::zeroinfl() or glmmTMB::glmmTMB()) get a heading row for each part.

References

Fox, J., & Monette, G. (1992). Generalized collinearity diagnostics. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 87(417), 178–183. doi:10.1080/01621459.1992.10475190

Examples

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + disp + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
apa_collinearity(fit)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   Variable `*VIF*` `95% CI for *VIF*` Tolerance
#>   <chr>    <chr>   <chr>              <chr>    
#> 1 Wt        5.37   [2.60,  7.30]      .19      
#> 2 Hp        3.53   [1.79,  4.80]      .28      
#> 3 Disp     12.90   [5.99, 17.49]      .08      
#> 4 Cyl       8.99   [4.43, 12.57]      .11      

# Bold VIFs of 10 or more, and show the note
apa_collinearity(fit, flag = 10) |>
  apa_note()
#> [1] "For Cyl, which has more than 1 *df*, *VIF* is the generalized *VIF* (Fox & Monette, 1992). Tolerance = 1/*VIF*, the proportion of a predictor's variance not explained by the other predictors. *VIF* = variance inflation factor; CI = confidence interval. *VIF*s of 10 or more are bolded."
